cards.title: Eratosthenes (c. 276 to c. 194 BCE)
cards.text: Eratosthenes worked in Alexandria, Egypt. About 240 BCE he compared the angle of the noon shadow in Alexandria with Syene (now Aswan), where the Sun was overhead at the same time of year. He used the distance between the two cities to estimate the Earth's circumference.
cards.limits: We know his method from later writers. The exact length of the 'stadion' he used is not known, so how accurate he was is still debated.

cards.title: Ibn al-Haytham (c. 965 to c. 1040)
cards.text: Ibn al-Haytham was born in Basra and worked in Cairo. In his Book of Optics (Kitab al-Manazir), he argued that we see because light comes from objects into the eye, and he used experiments to test claims about light.
cards.limits: 'The first scientist' is a modern title. People in many places tested ideas before him. The card does not show how his book was read in other places.

person.name: Ibn al-Haytham
person.region: West Asia and North Africa (Basra and Cairo)

cards.title: Bi Sheng (active 1040s)
cards.text: Shen Kuo's Dream Pool Essays (about 1088) describes how Bi Sheng, a commoner, made movable type from baked clay in the 1040s. Printing from carved wooden blocks was already in use in China before this.
cards.limits: This is one written description. No type made by Bi Sheng survives. Metal movable type was used later in Korea, and Gutenberg printed in Europe in the 1450s.

cards.title: Radhanath Sikdar (1813 to 1870)
cards.text: Radhanath Sikdar was a mathematician and 'computer' for the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India. Accounts credit him with calculations, about 1852, showing that Peak XV was higher than any peak measured before. The survey announced its height in 1856. The peak was later named after George Everest, a former head of the survey.
cards.limits: Exactly who did which calculation is debated, and the survey was team work. People who lived near the mountain already had names for it, such as Chomolungma in Tibetan.

cards.title: Alberto Santos-Dumont (1873 to 1932)
cards.text: Alberto Santos-Dumont was born in Brazil and worked in Paris. In 1906 he flew his airplane, the 14-bis, in Paris in front of a crowd and officials of the Aéro-Club de France. Many people in Brazil call him the inventor of the airplane.
cards.limits: In December 1903, Wilbur and Orville Wright flew a powered airplane at Kitty Hawk in the USA. Their flights had few witnesses and used a launching rail. Which flight counts as 'first' depends on the criterion.

cards.title: Kate Sheppard (1847 to 1934)
cards.text: In 1893 New Zealand became the first self-governing country in which all adult women had the right to vote in parliamentary elections. Kate Sheppard was a leader of the campaign, which sent large petitions to Parliament. Māori women also voted in 1893.
cards.limits: Some places had let some women vote earlier in local or limited elections. Women in New Zealand could not stand for Parliament until 1919. The campaign had many leaders, not one.

cards.title: Mary Wollstonecraft (1759 to 1797)
cards.text: Mary Wollstonecraft published A Vindication of the Rights of Woman in London in 1792. The book argued that women are rational beings and should have the education and rights to use their reason.
cards.limits: Earlier writers also defended women, for example Christine de Pizan in The Book of the City of Ladies (1405). The word 'feminist' came into use much later.
